+	// the resource received from the xDS server or an error indicating the
+	// reason why the resource cannot be obtained.
+	//

body:
Seeing it in a godoc server, this strikes me as a bad API design choice for Go.

I think `OnResourceChanged(ResourceData)` and `OnResourceError(error)` would be much nicer instead of a single method with a struct with one of two values that we have to do extra work to convince users will be set correctly.  It also eliminates a type from the package, making it smaller and easier to understand.

C++ has a nice `StatusOr` that works here, but Go doesn't support sum/union/algebraic/whatever types.  I think trying to force one to exist here is worse than having two methods.

I know the intent behind the gRFC design is to make it so this one method always updates the resource and the other method always doesn't.  But: 1. shaping the API that way doesn't force the implementer into doing it correctly, and 2. we can accomplish the same thing by documenting the (now) three methods accordingly.

cc: @markdroth @ejona86 thoughts?

> but Go doesn't support sum/union/algebraic/whatever types

Go supports it just fine for a use-case like this. You just have to have the fields be non-public. Just as in C++ and Java. Alternatively, you could have `OnResourceChanged(resource, err, processed)` if you wanted to reduce the number of structs.

> I think it will be more confusing for watcher implementers to understand... we're always going to have to remember that the Go API works differently in those discussions.

I'm not at all concerned about that. This is trivial. As long as the names clear (e.g., `ResourceChanged`, `ResourceChangedError`, `AmbientError`) it shouldn't be an issue, even cross-language. "Works differently" is either useless or a stretch; the encoding in this PR is just as different from C as Doug's proposal, in my mind. They have equivalent semantics.

(I'll note that Java doesn't have the OnCallbackProcessed argument, but we let the watcher specify a callback thread when registering. I'm surprised that it isn't synchronous in Go.)

I had this as my first proposal but we internally decided to follow the ResourceDataOrError like core.

I think ResourceChanged, ResourceChangedError, AmbientError is fine as long as names and documentation are clear. May be we can mention the these API(s) in gRFC A88 under implementation for go? I see that we do in some gRFCs like A72. @markdroth wdyt?
I'm not sure if we should link to this type. I'm not even sure if our authority corresponds to this type. I have never seen this proto before.

The order of the servers does not affect "high availability" in any way. The order of servers reflects the order of preference of the data returned by those servers. See: https://github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A71-xds-fallback.md#reservations-about-using-the-fallback-server-data

Also, maybe this file could be useful in terms of what to include in our docstrings: https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/grpc_xds_bootstrap_format.md

In general, I think there are two cases in which we should consider what behavior we want:
1. During normal operation of the LRS stream, when we get flow control push-back that prevents us from sending a message in a timely manner.
2. When all callers have unreffed the LoadStore and we need to flush the last queued data to the stream before we close the stream, but we get flow control push-back that prevents us from sending the message in a timely manner.

Both of these cases are fairly unlikely, and I would suggest that we don't actually implement any handling for these cases until/unless we have an actual need for them.  But it's worth thinking through how we would want to handle them if/when the time comes, just to make sure that we've left ourselves a way to extend the API to handle them without breaking anything.

Some questions to consider:
- Do we want the same timeout in both cases, or different timeouts?
- Do we want the timeouts tuned globally for the entire LrsClient, or do we want the ability to set them on a per-server basis?  Setting them globally implies they should be in this Config struct; setting them per-server implies that they would be part of the server specification that we pass to the ReportLoad() method.
- In case 2, if we hit the timeout, I think the right behavior is to just kill the stream and throw away the data that we couldn't send.  However, in case 1, we probably need to think a bit more about the right behavior -- the immediately obvious thing is to kill the stream and start a new one, hoping it will be better, but I don't know whether that is likely to improve the situation or whether it would just add more load to a server that's already trying to push back.  (The LRS stream itself is not going to be sending messages often enough to fill the flow control window, so the only cause I can think of here is the server being generally overloaded, which is not a condition that is specific to the individual stream.)  But if we could somehow both restart the stream and force choosing a new connection (which would potentially pick a different LRS server endpoint), that might be a better approach.  Also, note that whatever we do here, this is probably also something we'd want to fix in XdsClient as well.

in the current internal implementation, these are the sequence of steps

i) create the stream, send the initial LoadStatsRequest to LRS server
ii) receives the first LoadStatsResponse from LRS server and get the reporting interval.
iii) starts a goroutine (thread) to periodically send LoadStatsRequests.  The runner will restart the stream if it encounters any error.

So, i think we are doing what we described currently and we probably don't need a timeout for normal operation case 1) i.e. error while reporting load because in case of error the loads will be discarded and we will create a new stream and new goroutine which will get the load again and send as per report interval.

 > In case 2, if we hit the timeout, I think the right behavior is to just kill the stream and throw away the data that we couldn't send.
 
So, are you suggesting to not try to flush at all or try flushing the load data once and then kill the stream?

@dfawley if you are suggesting Stop() accepting a context, are you suggesting to start a new stream within Stop() to flush the current load? We will have the last stream open anyway, so we will just wait for the next reporting cycle to happen and then kill the stream. Where will we use this provided context?
I have removed the timeout field for lrs config for now. We can evaluate if we need a separate config param for this case or not during implementation of LRS client.

> starts a goroutine (thread) to periodically send LoadStatsRequests

What happens if we are supposed to send a load report every 10 seconds, but we get flow control push-back that prevents us from sending one of the messages on the stream for over a minute?  That's what I was referring to in case (1), and I think we might eventually want a timeout there.

Again, I am not saying that we need to actually add that timeout in this PR -- I agree with removing this field from the config.  But I do think we should make sure we structure the API in such a way that if we need to add this timeout in the future, we can do so without breaking the API.

> So, are you suggesting to not try to flush at all or try flushing the load data once and then kill the stream?

When the LoadStore loses its last ref, we should try to immediately send any queued stats that haven't yet been sent, and we should close the stream once that send is complete.  The timeout we might want here would be how long to wait for that send to complete before we give up and close the stream anyway.

This has some history on why we didn't want the `Equal` method that the `cmp` package can use.

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/pull/7757#discussion_r1810745576

For stop(), we decided to accept a context which user can provide with a timeout. So, we wait either wait for the last flush attempt to succeed or provided context to be done.

For the case 1) i think we only have cancelable object and if the connection is fine but there is flow control push back then we are hung. Not sure how common that case is though and if we want to proactively tackle it. We could have an internal timeout there but if we accept case 1) timeout from user, it will become difficult to handle the deref and keep track of timeouts of each caller. Perhaps we can think of doing it when we really need it?

Yes, as I've said a few times here, I don't think we should add this timeout as part of this current refactoring effort.  My only reason for bringing it up is to make sure that we have an idea of how we would add this timeout later, if/when the need arises.

To do that, I think we need to come to consensus on answers to the questions I posed above.
